clue.text: Revolutionary liquid oxygen carrier

parts.note: the fluid part of blood goes round the body's circulation, bearing the red cells that hold oxygen, so 'revolutionary' means circulating

explanation.surface: A rebel group's tanker of liquid oxygen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests a rebel, but here it means going round and round: blood circulates, and its liquid part carries the oxygen-bearing cells.
explanation.definitionFit: Plasma is the straw-coloured fluid of blood in which the cells are suspended as it circulates.

clue.text: Standard means to change fare from Italy

parts.note: par is the standard or normal level

indicators.note: to change means the letters of means are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A normal way to alter the menu at an Italian restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'means' looks like part of 'standard means' (a usual method), but it is the anagram fodder; 'fare' is food, not a ticket price.
explanation.definitionFit: This hard grated cheese from the Parma area is a classic food of Italy.

clue.text: Everybody at Ringway to see orthodox doctor

parts.note: all means everybody
the letter O is ring-shaped
a path is a way

explanation.surface: Everyone at Manchester's Ringway airport goes to see a conventional GP.
explanation.walkthrough: Ringway is the old name of Manchester Airport; here it splits into 'Ring' and 'way'.
explanation.definitionFit: An allopath practises mainstream medicine treating disease with opposing remedies, as opposed to a homeopath.

clue.text: Hardly a tricky call

parts.note: in card games such as solo whist, a bid undertaking to win no tricks at all, so a call that is not 'tricky'

explanation.surface: Hardly a difficult decision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tricky' reads as 'difficult', but it means 'taking tricks' at cards: this bid promises to take none.
explanation.definitionFit: In solo whist this declaration contracts to lose every trick, a call with no tricks in it.

clue.text: There's still water in fifty cent kettles

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'There's still water in fifty cent kettles': L (fifty) and DRUMS (kettles) are clear, but no reading of 'cent' gives the DO..D around L; likely an OCR or print garble with no scan to check.
annotationWithheld.clue: There's still water in fifty cent kettles

clue.text: Circular letter to fellow the Sultanate

parts.note: the letter O is a circle
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A round-robin letter sent to a man in the Gulf kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circular letter' suggests a round-robin mailing, but it is the letter shaped like a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabian state on the Gulf of Oman is ruled by a sultan.

clue.text: Describing line made by rulers?

parts.note: rulers here are monarchs, and the line is a royal succession, not a pencil stroke drawn with a straight-edge

explanation.surface: Drawing a straight line with rulers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'line made by rulers' pictures a straight-edge, but the rulers are kings and the line is a family of them.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for a succession of hereditary sovereigns from one family.

clue.text: Tear from bed, in revolt over the cause

indicators.note: over in a down clue places the first piece above the second

parts.note: people up in arms are in revolt
the root is the cause of something

explanation.surface: Rebels drag someone out of bed for the cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bed' suggests sleep, but it is a flower bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull a plant out of the ground, roots and all, is to tear it from its bed in the garden.

clue.text: Private papers destroyed

indicators.note: destroyed means broken up, so the letters of papers are put back together differently

explanation.surface: Confidential documents have been shredded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like an adjective about the papers, but it is a soldier's rank: a sapper is a private in the Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: A sapper is a rank-and-file soldier of the Royal Engineers.

clue.text: Sauce favour?

explanation.surface: A sauce offered as a party favour.
explanation.definitionFit: A relish is a piquant condiment, and to relish something is to like or enjoy it, to favour it.

clue.text: A little precipitation In Chopin's prelude

explanation.surface: A shower of rain falls during a piano recital of Chopin.
explanation.walkthrough: Chopin's Prelude in D flat, Op. 28 No. 15, is nicknamed the 'Raindrop' prelude for its repeated note like dripping water.
explanation.definitionFit: A single drop of rain is a tiny amount of rainfall, and the 'Raindrop' is the nickname of a famous Chopin piano prelude.

clue.text: To domineer over husband, female has to eat sparingly

parts.note: a hen is a female bird
to peck at food is to eat only a little

explanation.surface: A wife bosses her husband while picking at her food.
explanation.definitionFit: A wife who nags and bullies her spouse is said to keep him under her thumb.

clue.text: Erstwhile carrier and shipper

parts.note: erstwhile means former, as the prefix ex- does
a porter is someone who carries luggage

explanation.surface: Someone who used to haul goods and now ships them.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that sends goods abroad by sea is a shipper of trade overseas.

clue.text: A wild horse on the beach

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters of horse run loose into a new order

explanation.surface: A wild horse galloping along the sand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' makes OSHRE from the letters of HORSE, set after A.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on land rather than at sea, beside the water, is being on the beach.

clue.text: Elevated -situation of early rock music

parts.note: the lullaby 'Rock-a-bye baby' places the cradle high in a tree, the first rocking song a child hears

explanation.surface: Where pioneering rock and roll stood in its heyday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'early rock music' suggests 1950s rock and roll, but it is the nursery rhyme 'Rock-a-bye baby, on the ...', sung to rock an infant.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest branches of a tree, where the lullaby's cradle hangs, are a lofty spot.

clue.text: Play parts from the book

explanation.surface: Taking roles in a play adapted from a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play parts' looks like a verb phrase, but it is a noun: a play's parts are its acts.
explanation.definitionFit: A play is divided into acts, and the Acts of the Apostles is a book of the New Testament.

clue.text: It is on the right lines to find capital

definitions.text: It is on the right lines to find capital

parts.words: It is on the right lines to find capital
parts.note: read literally, a railway service running on the tracks that lead to the capital city, the direction British railways call 'up'

explanation.surface: Advice that someone is going the right way about raising money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the right lines' and 'capital' sound like finance; in Britain a train heading towards London is said to go 'up', so the hyphenated name is for a London-bound service.
explanation.definitionFit: On British railways, a service travelling towards London or a major terminus runs on the up line.

clue.text: Sr Pinero' troubled, having one inside?

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed, so the letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: The playwright Sir Arthur Pinero is upset at having someone locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubled' rearranges SRPINERO; 'one inside' is slang for someone in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: A person serving time behind bars is 'inside' in slang.

clue.text: First of the arched dreamers?

parts.note: the music-hall song 'Underneath the Arches' has its singers dream their dreams away there, and the duo who sang it were billed with this man first

explanation.surface: Who was the first to dream beneath vaulted arches?
explanation.walkthrough: Bud Flanagan and Chesney Allen, a British music-hall double act, made 'Underneath the Arches' famous; the first-named of the pair is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bud of that name was billed first in the music-hall duo who sang about dreaming under the arches.

clue.text: Tune Iris renders gets on one's nerves

indicators.note: renders means performs or makes into something, so the letters of these two words are turned into another arrangement

explanation.surface: The song Iris sings is irritating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets on one's nerves' reads as 'irritates', but it is literal: the condition sits on the nerves.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflammation of a nerve is an ailment that lodges in the nerves themselves.

clue.text: Novel game on the hearth?

parts.note: joins Dickens's Christmas book The ... on the Hearth with the bat-and-ball sport, as if a new game were played by the fire

explanation.surface: A new game to play by the fireside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as 'new', but it points to the Dickens story The Cricket on the Hearth; the sport of the same name is the game.
explanation.definitionFit: The bat-and-ball sport shares its name with the chirping insect of Dickens's fireside tale.

clue.text: Dismal university athlete

explanation.surface: A gloomy student sportsman.
explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford and Cambridge a blue is someone who has represented the university against the other in a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling low or depressed is feeling blue, and an Oxbridge sporting representative is awarded a blue.

clue.text: Boycott's remnant?.

parts.note: to boycott is to cut off dealings, and the phrase turned round names a leftover scrap of material

explanation.surface: What is left of Geoffrey Boycott's innings?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boycott' suggests the Yorkshire cricketer, but it means to cut someone off; reversing that phrase gives a leftover scrap.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of wood, cloth or paper left over after cutting is a remnant.

clue.text: Ply in London street …

explanation.surface: Plying a trade on a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: The Strand is a well-known street in central London.
explanation.definitionFit: A ply is a single thread twisted into a rope or yarn, and the Strand is a famous thoroughfare in London.

clue.text: … meeting-place in Broad Street

parts.note: read on from the previous clue: a spot where people gather sits inside the name for a wide tree-lined thoroughfare

explanation.surface: A gathering spot on a wide road.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on from 23 down; a broad street lined with trees holds within it the word for a meeting-place.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide street, often lined with trees, is a broad thoroughfare.

clue.text: Tricky thief's object of irrational reverence

indicators.note: tricky suggests something twisted and devious, so these letters are worked into another order

parts.note: the letters of thief's, with its S, form the fodder

explanation.surface: A crafty burglar's prized obsession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky' rearranges the six letters of THIEF'S; the apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A charm or object worshipped for supposed magical power is revered beyond reason.

clue.text: Memento of being bitter about first act of Julius Caesar

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece is placed around the other

parts.note: bitter means sour
Caesar's boast 'veni, vidi, vici' begins with veni, I came, his first act

explanation.surface: A keepsake from a bitter night watching the opening of Shakespeare's play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First act of Julius Caesar' suggests Shakespeare's play, but it is the first of Caesar's three deeds in 'I came, I saw, I conquered'.
explanation.definitionFit: A keepsake kept to recall a place or event is a reminder of it.

clue.text: Soft mineral found in em Emmental cheese

indicators.note: found in tells us the letters lie within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A soft rock discovered inside a Swiss cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of EmmenTAL Cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: This mineral, magnesium silicate, is the softest on the Mohs scale.

clue.text: Tea at home observed to be feller's equipment

parts.note: cha is a slang word for tea
in means at home
saw means observed

explanation.surface: Taking tea at home, someone is seen to be quite a fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feller' reads as a colloquial 'fellow', but it is one who fells trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A power tool with a toothed loop of chain is what a lumberjack uses to cut down trees.

clue.text: Champion to think back about-start of games

indicators.note: about means surrounding the letter from games
back tells us the word think is read backwards
start of games picks its opening letter

explanation.surface: A champion trying to recall something about the opening of the games.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns THINK into KNIHT, which goes round G from 'start of games'.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight was a medieval champion who fought on behalf of a cause or lady.

clue.text: Main current I created in a way

indicators.note: in a way suggests the letters are made into something else, a rearrangement of them

explanation.surface: Someone claims credit for a strong current in a roundabout sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is the sea, as in 'the Spanish Main'.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong current at sea caused by the tide is a rush of ocean water.

clue.text: Court exchanges seldom real these days

definitions.text: Court exchanges seldom real these days

parts.words: Court exchanges seldom real these days
parts.note: a rally on a court, played today mostly on lawn or hard courts rather than in the original indoor 'real' version

explanation.surface: A remark that courtroom testimony is rarely genuine now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' and 'exchanges' suggest a law court, but the court is for a racket game; real tennis is the original indoor form, now seldom played.
explanation.definitionFit: The racket game in which players exchange shots over a net is most often the lawn form, not the old real version.
